candidate.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — insulin pump safety / interrupted insulin delivery
candidate.educational_objective: Teach insulin-pump users that interruption of rapid-acting insulin delivery can quickly lead to hyperglycemia and ketosis/DKA, requiring prompt recognition and use of the prescribed backup/troubleshooting plan.

options.A: Because pumps deliver rapid- or ultra-rapid-acting insulin continuously, prolonged interruption can allow hyperglycemia and ketosis or diabetic ketoacidosis to develop quickly
options.B: A pump interruption is usually harmless for a full day because long-acting insulin remains under the skin
options.C: Insulin pumps eliminate the need to monitor glucose or respond to high-glucose alerts
options.D: If pump delivery stops, the client should avoid all insulin until the device can be professionally repaired

candidate.rationale: ADA 2026 Standards describe insulin pump therapy as continuous delivery of rapid- or ultra-rapid-acting insulin and specifically note the risk of rapid development of ketosis or diabetic ketoacidosis when insulin delivery is interrupted. Pump users therefore need education on monitoring and an individualized backup/troubleshooting plan. Pumps do not create a long-acting subcutaneous insulin depot, do not eliminate glucose monitoring, and interruption is not a reason to withhold needed insulin. Therefore A is the best answer.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Insulin pumps provide continuous rapid/ultra-rapid insulin; interruption can rapidly lead to ketosis or DKA, making prompt monitoring and troubleshooting essential.
